title: Replacing Legacy Terms: Real-Time Payouts API for Industrial Procurement
summary: Are 60-day payment terms costing you supplier goodwill? See how a real-time payouts API helps manufacturers pay faster and secure better materials.
body_markdown:
**Long payment terms squeeze suppliers and quietly cost the businesses that rely on them. This article looks at how faster payouts can strengthen procurement and what it takes to get started.**


Every procurement team knows the pattern. A purchase order goes out, materials arrive, the invoice is approved, and then the money waits 30, 60, or even 90 days. On paper, that delay looks like smart cash management. In practice, the cost lands on the people who keep your production line supplied.


Raw material suppliers run on thin margins and tight schedules. When they wait on payment, they delay their own purchases, tighten credit, and favor customers who pay faster. If your invoices are the slow ones, your orders can drift to the back of the line.


## What Slow Supplier Payments Really Cost Manufacturers


The problem goes beyond a few late invoices. A recent report on late payments among small manufacturers found that more than half of manufacturing suppliers receive payments late, with invoices taking nearly two months to settle on average. One delay then spreads into payroll, inventory purchases, and production schedules.


Paper habits play a part too. According to the[2025 AFP Digital Payments Survey](https://www.nacha.org/news/over-21-years-massive-drop-b2b-check-payments-study-finds) , checks now make up 26% of B2B payments, down from 81% in 2004. Businesses have largely moved on from paper, yet many still run approval and payment cycles that were built around it.


## Why a Real-Time Payouts API Fits Modern Procurement


The infrastructure is already in place.[Federal Reserve data](https://frbservices.org/resources/financial-services/fednow/quarterly-volume-value-stats) shows FedNow settled nearly 5 million payments in the second quarter of 2026, an 83% jump from the quarter before. It now counts[more than 1,800 participating banks and credit unions](https://www.digitaltransactions.net/fednow-marks-a-third-anniversary-tally-at-more-than-1800-banks-and-credit-unions/) . On the RTP side,[2026 network data](https://www.mastercard.com/us/en/news-and-trends/Insights/2026/powering-the-us-economy-with-real-time-payments.html) shows $481 billion in payments in the first quarter, up 195% from a year earlier, with more than 340,000 businesses using it to pay vendors. Both networks now allow up to $10 million per payment, so even large material orders fit.


A real-time payouts API connects your payables system to these rails. Once an invoice is approved, the payment can settle within seconds, on weekends and holidays included. That changes the conversation with suppliers in three ways:


- **Better pricing:** Suppliers paid at approval carry less financing cost and are often open to volume discounts.
- **Stronger relationships:** Predictable cash lets suppliers plan production and staffing with confidence.
- **Priority access:** When materials are scarce, the customer who pays reliably tends to get the first call.


## How Can a Company Make Its Supply Chain More Efficient?


Efficiency usually comes from removing waiting points. Shared inventory visibility, dependable supplier relationships, and fewer manual handoffs all help, but payment is often the last step still run by hand. Someone exports an approved invoice list, keys in bank details, and answers emails asking where the money is.


A payouts API automates that last step. Payments go out on a rule, supplier questions drop, and your finance team spends less time on follow-ups. Reliable and efficient payments are what keep every other improvement in the chain from stalling.


### What Process Refers to the Flow of Materials, Information, Payments, and Services From Raw Materials Suppliers to the Final Customer?


That process is supply chain management. Materials move toward the customer, information moves both ways, and payments move back toward the supplier. These flows depend on one another. When the payment flow slows down, suppliers cannot restock, ship, or extend credit, and the delay travels back down the line to your own production floor.
